messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Factory Worker
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Chantal was forty-two years old, a factory worker who had come to the United States from the Democratic Republic of Congo a decade ago, and she sat in the intake chair with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her face composed behind a careful mask of foundation and powder. She had been divorced for six years, and she lived alone in a small apartment near the industrial park where she operated a packaging machine. What had brought her to the clinic, she said, was that she could no longer sleep, and that she had started screaming at work when a co-worker named Emmanuel walked up behind her unexpectedly. She had not meant to scream. She had not meant to knock over the stack of boxes. But her body had moved before her mind caught up, and that was the part that frightened her most.

The event that had fractured her life happened in a different country, in a different season, but it lived inside her as if it were still happening. She had been detained by soldiers during a period of political unrest, held for three days in a concrete room with no windows. The men who questioned her had known her name. They had used it over and over, deliberately, almost gently, before the beatings began. The weather outside had been humid and heavy, the kind of thick heat that pressed down on the chest and made it hard to breathe, and the smell of sweat and diesel fuel and something metallic had soaked into her clothes, her hair, her skin. She had been released eventually, but she had never told anyone the full story. The memory was so extreme it was hard to believe it had actually happened to her. Sometimes she thought it felt like a film she had watched, or a story someone else had told her. The memory felt alien, as if it belonged to a woman she no longer was. And yet, when she let her mind drift for even a moment, she could smell it again—the diesel, the metal, the sweat—as vividly as if she were still in that room.

In the years since, Chantal had built a life around staying safe, though she would not have described it that way. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined her—the things that had made her feel competent and strong, like walking home after dark, or trusting a stranger, or letting herself feel tired without immediately forcing her mind to something else. She kept her mind occupied all the time. At work, she listened to music through earbuds and focused on the rhythm of the machine. At home, she cleaned, she watched television, she scrolled through videos on her phone until her eyes burned. She never let herself sit in silence. Silence was when her body started to react before her mind had even had time to think. A car door slamming outside, the hum of a refrigerator kicking on, the creak of a floorboard in the hallway—ordinary sounds that would not bother most people made her jump, made her heart hammer, made her freeze in place and listen for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home.

She had also learned to manage her appearance as a form of protection. She wore heavy makeup every day, a thick layer of foundation and powder that felt like armor. She did not know exactly when this had started, only that she had come to feel exposed without it, as if her face were too readable, as if someone might see the fear written there and use it against her. She also avoided wearing clothes that resembled what she had worn during those three days—a dark blue blouse and a wraparound skirt. She had thrown them away years ago, but the memory of the fabric against her skin still made her stomach turn. She had bought new clothes, all in different colors and cuts, but she still checked every item before putting it on, scanning for anything that might feel too familiar.

The consequences of these habits had accumulated slowly. Her divorce had been partly about the distance she had created, the way she could never fully be present, the way she startled when her husband touched her shoulder. She had lost contact with most of her friends. She had stopped going to church, stopped attending community gatherings. At work, she had been written up twice for missing shifts—days when the weather matched the heavy humidity of that week, days when she could not bring herself to leave the apartment. She had called in sick those days, but the real reason was that the air itself felt dangerous, and she could not trust her own body to carry her through an eight-hour shift without collapsing.

What had finally pushed her to seek help was the incident with Emmanuel. She had screamed, and everyone had turned to look at her, and she had seen the confusion and pity in their faces. She had gone home that evening and sat on the edge of her bed, and for the first time in years she had let herself think about what it might mean to live without this constant vigilance. She was afraid of what the therapy might unearth. She was afraid that if she stopped monitoring the world for threats, she would be caught off guard, that something terrible would happen. But she was also tired, more tired than she had ever been, and she wanted to believe that her body could be something other than a source of fear.
